M. H. Khondaker, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, (M/s. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury and Fazlul Huq, Advocates, Supreme Court with him), instructed by Md. Sajjadul Huq, Advocate on Record ------ For the Appellant. 
M/s. Asrarul Hossain and Md. Jane Alam, Senior Advocates, Supreme Court, Sk. Abul Hossain, Advocate Supreme Court, with him), instructed by S. M. Huq, Advocate on Record ------ For Respondents No. 2 to 4.
parties:
Nurjahan Begum wife of Mahmudur Rahman ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Mahmudur Rahman Mullick being dead his heirs and legal representatives: - Musammat Nurjahan Begum first wife already on record as Defendant appellant and others ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27-11-79 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 140 of 1965)
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam; J.- This appeal by special leave arises from the judgment and decree of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 140 of 1965 affirming those of the Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 43 of 1963.

2. Plaintiff Mahmudur Rahman Mullick, since dead, filed the title suit against the appellant his wife for declaration that the plaintiff is the real owner of half of the properties described in schedule 'A' and owner of 14 83/194 annas share of the properties described in schedule 'B' to the plaint; and for a further declaration that the defendant (appellant) has no right, title, interest and possession in the said properties on the basis of the deeds taken in her name. The plaintiff made an alternative prayer for khas possession if he be found to be out of possession of the properties in suit.

3. Plaintiff's case in short is that he married the defendant in 1933 but had no issue. On June 6, 1945, the plaintiff purchased the premises No. 207A, Park Street, Calcutta for Rs. 36,750/- with his own money, and the kabala was taken in the name of his wife, that is, the defendant. The plaintiff purchased the undivided 33/13 annals share of the premises Nos. 25, 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta from defendant's sisters on March 10, 1951 for Rs. 28,800/-which was paid out of his own fund and the kabala was taken in the name of the defendant. The plaintiff purchased undivided 39/260 annas share of the premises No. 25, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta for Rs. 5,000/- and of the premises Nos. 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta for Rs. 3,000/- from Wazidur Rahman (brother of defendant) on January 15, 1954. The plaintiff also purchased the same share of the said properties for Rs. 5,000/- and Rs. 3,000/- from Mazidur Rahman and Azizur Rahman (two other brothers of defendant) on February 26, 1954 and May 4, 1954 respectively. Plaintiff's further case is that while possessing and enjoying the said properties acquired by him with his own fund, he exchanged the aforesaid Dum Dum Road properties with schedule 'B' properties in Dacca of Maran Chand Sea Zohari; and that he exchanged the premises No. 207A, Park Street, Calcutta for half share of the premises Nos. 12/1 and 12/2, Farashganj Road, Dhaka (schedule 'A') belonging to Rama Nath Das. He also stated that at all material times he was in possession of the properties in suit and the title deeds were in his custody but the defendant wrongfully took away the same during his short absence from Dacca between August 7, 1962 and September 6, 1962. This led the plaintiff to file the suit.

4. The defendant-appellant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. Her case, shortly stated, is that the premises No. 207A, Park Street, Calcutta was purchased by her with her own money. Her husband (plaintiff) used to look after her affairs. The plaintiff had no money at that time to purchase the property. Premises No. 25, 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta were the paternal houses of the defendant and when her sisters wanted to transfer their shares the defendant purchased the same with her own money. Similarly, the defendant claimed that she also acquired the interests of her brothers Wazidur Rahman and Mazidur Rahman for Rs. 5,000/- and Rs. 3,000/- and the consideration was paid from her own fund. With regard to the share of Azizur Rahman, she claimed that the property was acquired not by purchase but by exchange. Further case of the defendant is that regarding the Dum Dum Road and Park Street properties there was a suit for partition being Title Suit No. 163 of 1949 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Adipose, 24-Parganas, instituted by the defendant's three sisters and one brother in which the defendant and the plaintiff were impleaded as defendant No. 4 and defendant No. 9 respective. The plaintiff of the said suit ultimately gave up their claims acknowledging the title of defendant No. 4 (the present appellant) in the said suit. The properties acquired and possessed by the defendant were exchanged with the properties in suit for her own interest and all the title deeds are with her. Her husband merely helped her in these affairs. The properties were duly mutated in the Municipal register and in the Revisional Survey Settlement and her name has been recorded as the owner of the said properties acquired by exchange. She paid the government revenue and municipal taxes regularly. That the plaintiff had no interest in the said property nor he ever claimed any such interest will be evident from the property statement made by him to the Income-Tax Department. He never included those properties in that statement. Her further case is that she entered into an agreement with Rama Nath Das for the exchange of the entire property of schedule 'A' but on the request of the plaintiff and his two brothers she agreed to take half share of the property with a view to providing accommodation to her father-in-law's family at Dacca, and as such the exchange document was made in her favour to the extent of 8 annas share and the plaintiff and his two brothers got the remaining 8 Anna’s share. The plaintiff and his brothers became co-sharer in the property without paying any consideration, and it was given to them out of love and affection and for maintaining good relationship between the parties. Her further case is that gradually the relationship between the defendant and the plaintiff became strained when the plaintiff took a second wife and started living in a separate house, but the defendant continued to possess and maintain and manage her own properties by herself. According to her the suit was speculative one. She also alleged that the suit was filed with the malafide object of depriving the defendant of the properties acquired and possessed by her. In this context she also alleged that the plaintiff started ill-treating her and attempted to assault her and this led her to take recourse to Criminal Court under section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and proceedings, was drawn up against the plaintiff. Then their relationship further deteriorated. The defendant believed that the suit had been filed to dishonor and humiliate her and to extort money from her. She also alleged that the plaintiff took away all her jewelries which were kept in the safe custody of Habib Bank Limited, Dacca. She also stated that because of the bitter feelings developed between them she did not allow the plaintiff to live in the premises No. 12, Farashganj Road, Dacca where she has been living and the plaintiff lived in a separate house at Mitford Road, Dacca with his second wife

5. On consideration of the evidence led by the parties the learned Subordinate Judge accepted the case of the plaintiff that the properties were acquired in the benami of his wife. Nurjahan Begum. With regard to property at Park Street, Calcutta he found that it was the plaintiff who paid the consideration of the said property which was acquired in the benami of his wife Nujahan Begum. With regard to Dum Dum Road properties acquired by kabala Exhibits 1 (b) to 1 (g) relating to the shares of the defendant's three brothers and sisters the learned 'Subordinate Judge found that consideration money was paid by the plaintiff and the properties were acquired for his own interest. In short, the learned Subordinate Judge accepted in to the benami case as given out by the plaintiff. With regard to the exchange of the said properties with the properties in suit the learned Subordinate Judge also accepted the case of the plaintiff that the suit properties were acquired by the plaintiff by exchange of his Park Street and Dum Dum Road properties. With regard to payment of consideration money the learned Subordinate Judge found that the defendant had no fund and consideration money was paid by plaintiff out of his own fund. On these findings the learned Sub-ordinate Judge made the declaration that the properties in suit were acquired by the plaintiff with his own fund in the benami of his wife, the defendant. With regard to possession the learned Subordinate Judge confirmed plaintiff's possession in all the suit properties except residence portion of 12, Farashganj Road, Dacca wherein the defendant is living. He directed that the plaintiff will get possession of the residence portion of 12, Farashganj Road, Dacca jointly with the defendant.

6. Against this decision the defendant preferred an appeal before the High Court at Dacca, raising several questions of law and fact the learned Judges of the Division Bench, however, affirmed the decision of the trial Court and dismissed the appeal.

7. Leave was granted to examine whether the question of benami has been correctly decided by the trial Court and the High Court Division, particularly in view of admission of the plaintiff in the suits filed by the brothers and sisters of the defendant in the Alipore Court, that the property at 207A, Park Street was exclusively owned by the defendant as her self-acquired property.

<u>8. In a benami transaction the real owner of a property allows it to appear in the name of an ostensible owner, himself remaining the beneficiary of the property. The practice of benami developed in the Indian sub-continent long before its conquest by the Muslim and during the Muslim rule the practice of benami received full recognition from the authorities and the Courts as well. That the practice of benami was widely practiced throughout the sub-continent is evident from the early history of the East India Company. The company started administering the province of Bengal in 1757. Law reports of cases involving benami transaction decided by the Sudder Diwany Adawlat and the Supreme Court of Bengal amply show that the benami system became an institution which was accepted in the common parlance though the Judges used to refer to it as a "pernicious system" but were obliged to recognise it and give effect to such transactions which were otherwise valid. In 1882 the practice of benami received formal legislative recognition when the Indian Trust Act (Act II of 1882) was enacted. The ostensible owner or the benamidar holds the property in trust for the real owner, relationship between benamidar and the real owner is that of a trustee and ‘cestui que trust'. Thus the 'cestui que trust' became the beneficial owner of its property. The custom and habit of the people in this sub-continent acquiring property benami may be attributed to several causes, some of the important causes as noticed by the authorities, may be enumerated as follows :—</u>

<u>(1) The Hindu joint family system;</u>

<u>(2) The innate desire to preserve property and evade the rules against perpetuities;</u>

<u>(3) Fraud, fear and risk of expropriation in a society in which might was right;</u>

<u>(4) Avoidance of annoyance from rulers and armed enemies;</u>

<u>(5) Desire to conceal the extent of one's wealth;</u>

<u>(6) The parda system, that is, the seclusion of women.</u>

9. Benami transfers may be classified in two classes of transactions. Transfers where the real owner of the property transferred to another without any intention whatever to benefit the transferee and no consideration passing from the transferee to the transferor formed one class. In such transfers the transferor remains to be the real owner but he holds property in the name of the transferee. The other class consists of transfers where a person purchases property in the name of another person. In such transfers, there is a real transaction and the purchaser, who pays the consideration money, acquires the property for his own benefit, and the person whose name appears in the deed of transfer, merely lends his name to the transaction, and acquires no interest in the property.

10. The law of benami was reviewed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the cases of Gopeekrist Gossain Vs. Gungapershad Gossain (1854) 6 Moore's Indian Appeal 53, which is still held to be authority in dealing, with benami transactions. The principle laid down in the above mentioned case which arose exclusively from Hindu law, was applied in transactions between the Muslims,

<u>11. In a benami transaction source of purchase money is an important criteria but it is not conclusive. The initial presumption in the case of a transfer concluded by a registered deed is in favour of the person whose name appears as the transferee in the deed, but this presumption is rebuttable. Source of consideration money though an important criteria in a benami transaction but in the absence of an unambiguous ownership consideration of other relevant circumstance's become important in a case where ownership is disputed. The disputed question of benami cannot be determined only on the consideration of source of consideration money, and it becomes incumbent for the Court to fall back upon the surrounding circumstances of the transaction, the position of the parties and the relationship to each other. The motive which could govern their actions, but their subsequent conduct including their dealings and the enjoyment of the property become relevant factors for consideration. In the case of Musammat Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh (1915) L.R. 42 I.A. 202 the Privy Council while adopting the principle as laid down in Gopeekrist Gossain's case, that the criterion in benami cases is the source of money with which the consideration was paid, made an important qualification, in that the source of purchase money is only to be the criterion in the absence of all other relevant circumstances. Among other circumstances possession of the property has been held to be very important. The Privy Council in Imambandi Begum Vs. Kumleshwari Pershad (1886) L. R. 13 l.A. 160 held as under :-</u>

<u>"Where there are benami transactions and I the question is who is the real owner, the actual possession or receipt of rents of the property is most important."</u>

<u>In the case of Ram Narain Vs. Muhammad Hadi (1898) L.R. 26 l.A. 38 the Privy Council laid stresses on the factum of possession of the property .and the collection of rents. Incidentally it may be mentioned that in a disputed case of benami, custody of the documents is a relevant factor to be considered.</u>

12. In the instant case the plaintiff married the defendant in the year 1933 but had no issue. According to the plaint case, June 6, 1945 he purchased the premises No. 207A, Park Street, Calcutta for Rs. 36,750/- with his own money and his own interest but the kabala was taken in the benami of his wife, the defendant. Further case of the plaintiff is that he purchased undivided 33/13 annas share of the premises No. 25, 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta from his wife's sisters on March 10, 1951 for Rs. 28,800/- out of his own fund but the kabala was taken in the name of his wife. According to him, he purchased undivided 3(9/260) anns share of the premises No. 25, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta for Rs. 5000/- and the premises No. 23A and 23B of Dum Dum Road, Calcutta for Rs. 3,000/- from Wazidur Rah-man, brother of the (defendant) on June 15, 1954. The plaintiff similarly purchased the same share of the same premises for Rs. 5,000/- and Rs. 3000/- from Mazidur Rahman and Azizur Rahman ( two other brothers of the defendant) of the said three premises of Dum Dum Road on February 26, 1954 and May 4, 1954. respectively. The plaintiff's assertion is that he purchased the property with his own money but the kabalas were taken in the name of his wife. The plaintiff alleged that while exercising all acts of possession and ownership exclusively in respect of the properties acquired by him, he exchanged those properties with the properties described in the schedules 'A' and 'B' to the plaint on July 21, 1954 and December 13, 1955 respectively. He further alleged that at all material times he has been the rightful owner in possession of the property in suit. With regard to the title deeds of the properties in dispute the plaintiff alleged that during his temporary absence from Dacca between August 7, 1962 and September 6, 1962 the defendant took away the same, for which he lodged a First Information Report to the police. Defendant contended that she was never the benamidar of the plaintiff relating to the suit properties, and she claimed that the suit properties and the relevant documents regarding title to the properties in suit are all along in the possession of the defendant in her own right; and the defendant is realising rent in her own name and maintaining accounts since her purchase in the normal course of events. She also contended that the suit is a speculative one. According to her the Park Street property was purchased by her with her own money and she possessed it. The premises No. 25, 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road Calcutta were paternal houses of the defendant and when her sisters wanted to transfer their shares she purchased the same in her own name and she paid the consideration money from her personal fund. The shares of her brothers Wazidur Rahman and Mazidur Rahman were also acquired by her with her own money. So far as the share belonging to her brother Azizur Rahman, it was acquired not by purchase but by exchange with her Khulna property. She, however, admitted that her husband used to manage her properties. Both sets of properties, namely, Park Street property and Dum Dum Road property were exchanged with the properties mentioned in the schedules 'A' and 'B' to the plaint in her name. She claimed that after acquiring the suit properties by ex-change she has been possessing and enjoying the income therefrom. In support of her claim to the property as the owner she adduced evidence and produced all the relevant title deeds, papers and accounts.

<u>13. On perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division affirming that of the trial Court, it appears that the suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff mainly on consideration of source of money paid as the consideration. Practically no importance has been given to the other surrounding circumstances, namely, the position of the parties and their relationship to each other, the motive for acquiring the properties in the benami, subsequent conduct of the parties relating to enjoyment of the property, etc.</u>

14. The Park Street property was purchased from one Md. Nasiruddin by a kabala Exhibit No. 1 dated June 6, 1945 for a consideration of Rs. 36,750/-, paid, as the memo of consideration recited in the kabala indicates, by two cheques drawn by plaintiff in favour of the vendor, the first one dated March 22, 1945 for Rs. 5,000/- and second one dated May 11, 1945 for Rs. 31,750/- Thekabala was executed on March 22, 1945 and registered on May 12, 1945. The plaintiff produced the counterfoils of the cheques to show that it was he who drew the cheques, He also produced counterfoils of another cheque of Rs. 1,471/- issued in favour of the vendor Md. Nasiruddin, which, according to the plaintiff, was paid towards the cost of the kabala. The plaintiff also produced the statement of bank accounts Exhibit No 3 and 3(a) to show that, he had sufficient money in his account and the cheques issued by him were duly encased,

15. Beside the recitals in the kabala showing the mode of payment of the consideration money and the counterfoils of the cheques and the statement of accounts, the plaintiff examined himself to prove his case relating to payment of the consideration money of the Park Street property. He also examined two of his office 'karmacharies' to prove his case as P.Ws. 2 and 3. None of them was an eyewitness of the transaction. On careful perusal of the deposition of the plaintiff it appears that he stated that he purchased the Park Street property from one Md. Nasiruddin on June 6, 1945 on the basis of the deed of transfer Exhibit No. 1, but curiously enough there is no statement asserting that he purchased the property in the benami of his wife, the defendant. It does not appear even that he asserted that the defendant was his benamidar. None of the two witnesses examined by him, witnessed the transaction of acquiring the Park Street property. They stated that subsequent to the transfer of Park Street property they were told by the plaintiff that he purchased the property with his own money and for his own benefit. On consideration of the recitals in the kabala showing mode of payment of the consideration money and the statement of account from the Bank the learned Judges arrived at the finding that it was plaintiff who paid the consideration money for the Park Street property and he purchased the property in the benami of his wife. The defendant in her evidence made a categorical statement that a sum of Rs. 50,000/- was given to her by her father Kanchan Munshi a few days before the transfer was completed, she kept the money with the plaintiff and out of that amount the plaintiff paid the consideration money by issuing cheques in favour of the vendor Md. Nasiruddin. In cross-examination with regard to his claim of payment of the consideration for the, Park Street property, it was put to the plaintiff that payment was made out of the money he received from his wife and that his bank account was utilized for making the payment. With reference to the statement of the plaintiff's bank accounts it was also put to the plaintiff that in course of management of defendant's property her money used to come to his hand by way of collection and that he kept that money sometimes in his account. In course of his cross examination he could not give the source of the sums deposited in his account, that is, Rs. 3,000/- on March 12, 1945, Rs. 3,000/- on March 23, 1945, Rs, 16,900/- on March 23, 1945, Rs. 3,299/- on March 26, 1945 and Rs. 17,327/- on April 6, 1945. The plaintiff, however, admitted that by virtue of these deposits in March and April he could issue a cheque for Rs. 31,750/- to Md. Nasiruddin on May 11, 1945.

16. The defendant stated her case in paragraph 9 of the written statement asserting that the property was purchased with her own money. She explained that her father was a rich man and occasionally he used to give money out of love and affection. He was a big business man and owned vast properties in Calcutta and in the district of Jessore and the defendant being the elder daughter he used to pay her large sums of money from time to time and with her own money she purchased the Park Street property. The plaintiff being the husband of the defendant used to look after her affairs The defendant stoutly denied that the kabala was taken in her benami by the plaintiff. In her deposition she stated that she purchased the Park Street property during the lifetime of her father, and her father gave this amount. D.W Sakina Khatun, sister of the defendant while deposing ID support of the defendant's case stated that My father purchased this property for Nurjahan. My father paid the consideration money of Park Street property". In cross-examination this witness stated that she asked her father how Nurjahan got the Park Street, property. At this- he said that he purchased that property for  Nurjahan D.W. Wazidur Rahman, brother of the defendant, stated that the land at 207A. Park Street Road was purchased by the defendant Nurjahan from Nasiruddin. The purchase, money of the said property was given to her by his father Kanchan Munshi, Kanchan Munshi told him about the giving of the consideration money. The said amount was given to Nurjahan to purchase the land. He stoutly denied that the plaintiff purchased this land with his own/money in the benami of Nurjahan. While considering this evidence the learned Subordinate Judge remarked that the version as contained in paragraph 9 of the written statement and the version as given out by the defendant in her deposition are not consistent. The version given out by Sakina Khatun and Wazidur Rahman belies the case of the defendant and it does not support the version given out by the defendant either in her pleading or in her deposition.

The learned Judges of the High Court Division practically affirmed this finding without any independent examination of the relevant evidence. On careful examination of different versions given, in the pleadings and in the deposition, as indicated above, we find that the statements' actually do not appear to be inconsistent as remarked, by the learned Subordinate Judge and the learned Judges of the High Court Division. For proper appreciation of the question relevant portion of paragraph 9 of the written statement' is quoted below:

"The property was purchased by the defendant with her own money. Her father was a rich man, besides he was a big business man and owned vast properties in Calcutta and in the District of Jessore and the defendant being the elder daughter was paid large sums of money from time to time and the defendant with her own money had purchased the Park Street property".

The defendant in her deposition stated as follows:

"I purchased the Park Street land during the life time of my father. I have purchased the Park Street land from Mr. Nasiruddin. I have purchased the land with Rs. 36,750/- in total This amount my father gave me".

D. W. 4 Atiur Rahman stated that the defendant had property at Park Street. She purchased the same from Nasiruddin. Her father gave her money. D.W. Wazidur Rahman stated in his deposition as follows:-

"Before that Nurjahan had another property at Park Street in Calcutta. This was a plot of land purchased by Nurjahan. She purchased it from Nasiruddin. The purchase money of the said property was given to her by my Father kanchan munshi, My father told me about the giving of this money to Nurjahan. The said amount was given to Nurjahan to purchase land". D.W. Sakina Khatun stated as follows:

"Besides the shares in the properties purchased from us Nurjahan had her own property at Park Street in Calcutta. My father purchased this property for Nurjahan. My father paid the consideration money for Park Street property."

The versions as appearing from the depositions quoted above do not support the finding that the story given out by the defendant with regard to purchase of Park Street property in her pleadings and in her deposition are inconsistent. Common feature in the above statements is that Kanchan Munshi paid the amount to the defendant with which the defendant paid consideration money for purchasing the Park Street property. It would not be correct to say that it is not the case of the defendant that she purchased the Park Street property with the money paid by her father Kanchan Munshi, and the version given by D.W. Atiur Rahman in Court is altogether a new case as remarked by the learned Subordinate Judge.

17. Relying on the evidence as indicated above the learned Subordinate. Judge arrived at the finding on the question of source of money and accepted the case of the plaintiff that the consideration money was paid by him for his own benefit; and that the purchase was made by the plaintiff in the benami of his wife, the defendant. I do not consider that the evidence produced by the plain tiff was sufficient to rebutt the presumption that the purchaser shown in the kabala Exhibit 1 was the real purchaser. However, this question is to be considered along with the evidence produced by the defendant in support of her case that the Park Street property was purchased by her with her own money, and she was not benamidar of the Plaintiff. The learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the defendant's case that she made the' payment of the consideration money for acquiring Park Street property out of the sum of Rs. 50,000/- given by her father, Kanchan Munshi. It appears from the judgment that the learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the defendant's case of payment of the consideration money mainly on the view that. at the relevant time Kanchan Munshi was not went off to pay defendant a sum of Rs. 50,000-/ and while considering this aspect he referred to some of the documents produced by the plaintiff but he did not at all refer to the evidence of Wazidur Rahman, one of the sons of Kanchan Munshi. D.W. Wazidur Rahman gave particulars of the properties and the business owned by Kanchan Munshi. He stated that his father Kanchan Munshi owned and possessed about 600 bighas of paddy lands in his native village at Kamargram now within the district of Faridpur. This property is still there with Wazidur Rahman. Kanchan Munchi had three houses at the three holdings at 25, 2?A and 238, Dum Dum Road, Calcutta. These are pucca houses and No. 25 holding was two storied 'building. Both the holding Nos. 23A and 23B were three storied. Kanchan Munshi used to reside at No. 25 house. The houses of Dum Dum Road were within the Calcutta Corporation. Kanchan Munchi also had a house at 15/2, Raja Manindra Road. This one was pucca building. Kanchan Munshi had three houses at 1/1, 1/2 and 1/3, Dum Dum Road at Shabjibagan Basti. These were with pucca floor. Kanchan Munshi had fishery and a garden at Gouripur. There were 12 bighas of land in the garden with house which was a one storied building. Kanchan Munshi had also 50/60 bighas of paddy land at Matcal. He had 150 bighas of paddy lands at Gobra within 24- Parganas and there was a garden house having 15/16 bighas of land with one storied building containing 8 rooms in it. Kanchan Munshi used to serve in the Andrew Yule and Co. Calcutta as Marine Superintendent with a salary of Rs. 300/-p.m. Wazidur Rahman further stated besides this his father had many businesses. There was a shop under the name Indian Paint Supply at Barabazar and its telephone No. was Calcutta 791 which was being used by the plaintiff. Kanchan Munshi had 6 Steel Boats and with these he used to have Jute Bale binding and loading and unloading work. Kanchan Munshi was also a labour contractor of Hanuman Jute Mills. He had a Roof Factory at Burhanpur. He had a vegetables. Arat near Ultadangar Khal Kanchan Munshi had a cloth shop under the name of ‘Jessore Store' at R.G. Kar Road. He had another cloth shop named 'K.B. Store' at R.G. Kar Road. Kanchan Munshi was also owner of a Cinema Hall named Rup Mandir at Ghugudanga. The statements of Wazidur Rahman with regard to property and business owned by Kanchan Munshi remained uncontroverted and there was no cross-examination even to, refute it. These statements practically stand unchallenged. Even the properties and business owned by Kanchan Munshi as admitted by the plaintiff in his cross-examination lend sufficient support to the defendant's case that Kanchan Munshi was a rich man owning quite substantial quantity of properties having good income. From the judgment it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the defendant's case of payment of Rs. 50,000/-by her father before her purchase of Park Street property mainly on consideration of Exhibit 19 certified copy of deposition of kanchan Munshi in Suit No. 816 of 1943 of the High Court of Calcutta dated July 31, 1945. He remarked that it is no doubt true that Kanchan Munshi was an enterprising man but he was exhausted and had no means to pay as claimed by the defendant. Exhibit 19 shows that one Kamal Ahmed sued Karimunnessa Bibi wife of Kanchan Munshi to recover Rs. 3,000/- and odd being the around due for the price of work done and labour supplied in the construction of a building raised by Karimunnessa Bibi. Construction work was done some time in 1939 and a sum of Rs. 660/- remained outstanding, and this amount was not paid and the plaintiff filed the suit. From the nature of question and answer as contained in Exhibit 19 it appears that Kanchan Munshi engaged Kamal Ahmed (plaintiff) to do some electrical work in connection with a big building constructed at a cost about 1 lakh and half. A. sum of Rs. 660/- remained due from him on account of said electrical work. This amount was not paid on the day the work was completed due to shortage of fund. Kanchan Munshi, however, explained that he had not sufficient money to pay him only on the first day and second day; and that balance amount could not be paid. as the plaintiff could not be traced. The question and answer do not lead to the conclusion that Kanchan Munshi was an exhausted man and he had no means to pay his debts. The learned Subordinate Judge on the basis of the above mentioned depositions observed as follows :—

"In that deposition Kanchan Munshi himself pleaded in July, 1945 that he had no means to pay even a paltry sum of Rs. 760/-. It is really ridiculous to say that he paid a sum of Rs. 50,000/- to his daughter a month earlier".

18. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have totally misconceived the purport of the deposition of Kanchan Munshi in Suit No. 816 of 1943. From his answers .it cannot be said that Kanchan Munshi made an admission to the affect that he had no means to pay Rs. 760/- in 1945. From the decree passed in the said suit Exhibit 20 it appears that the entire claim in that suit was, paid amicably out of Court. On consideration of the evidence and the relevant materials on record I find, it difficult to agree with the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge which has been affirmed by the learned Judges of the High Court Division to the effect that- Kanchan Munshi was an exhausted man in 1945 and for him to pay Rs, 50,000/- to the defendant was highly improbable. The plaintiff produced statements of his bank accounts Exhibit 3 and 3 (a) to show that no such amount of Rs. 50,000/- was deposited by him in any of his accounts, and if any such sum of Rs. 50,000/- was handed over by the defendant after she got it from her father Kanchan Munshi, the money would have been deposited in his account. The statements of account do not show any deposit of Rs. 50,000/- by the plaintiff. But the statements show that in one of the two accounts, during the period from March 13, and May 12, 1945 in total Rs. 43,526/- was deposited. The plaintiff in his deposition could not explain the source of the sums deposited on different dates. Although according to him he had no other income other than the income shown in the Income-Tax return for the relevant year.

19. It is true that the defendant could not lead independent evidence to prove payment of Rs. 50,000/- by Kanchan Munshi to her before her purchase of Park Street property from Md. Nasiruddin, but her brother and sisters who deposed at the trial supported her case that Kanchan Munshi paid the money to the defendant for purchasing Park Street property. On consideration of all these materials on record I find that payment of Rs. 50,000/- has been disbelieved by the learned Subordinate Judge as well as by the learned Judges of the High Court Division without proper assessment of evidence; and the finding on the question of payment of consideration money by the defendant for purchasing Park Street property is not warranted by the evidence on record. Mr. M. H. Khondkar, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants rightly made a grievance that the findings on the basis of which the suit has been decreed in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained on proper consideration of the evidence. Although determination of this question involved examination of the evidence, but it could not be avoided. I examined the evidence while considering the question whether plaintiff succeeded in rebutting the presumption that the defendant being the ostensible, owner was the real owner of the property.

20. Plaintiff claimed that he purchased the shares of brothers and sisters of defendant in, the Dum Dum Road property left by Kanchan Munshi comprising premises No. 25, 23A and 23B by kaba1as Exhibits 1 (a) to 1(g), and in support of his claim he produced certified copies of the sale deeds. By the kabala Exhibit I (a) the plaintiff claims to have purchased the shares of three step-sisters of Nurjahan Begum. Consideration money was paid by three bank drafts out of his own fund and he obtained the kabala for his own interest in the name of his wife Nurjahan Begum. According to the defendant, the shares of her two step-sisters, were acquired by her out of her own fund. In her pleadings she stated that she purchased the shares of her sisters at a consideration of Rs. 28,800/- when they wanted to sell their shares of their paternal houses, to protect her interest, as she was holding some shares in the property as an heir of late Kanchan Munshi. Regarding source of money she stated that she got the money from her mother Karimunnessa. Kabala Exhibit 1(a) shows that the consideration money / wasp aid by 3 bank drafts issued from National Bank of Pakistan, Khulna Branch. According to the plaintiff the vendors wanted the consideration money in Pakistan currency equivalent to Endian Rs. 28,800/-. He obtained these bank drafts from Pakistani Bank and handed over the same to the vendors. Sakhina Khatun, one of the vendors stated that she and her two other sisters Mehernegar and Amina Khatun sold their entire share in the Dum Dum property to the defendant at Rs. 28,800/-. They got the consideration money from the defendant in cash, and they kept the amount of Rs. 28,800/-with the plaintiff. The sisters were given three receipts for the amount by the plaintiff, each one for Rs. 6,666/-. The three bank drafts were handed over to them when they came to Dacca. Defendant's case that she got this money from her mother Karimunessa has been disbelieved by the learned Subordinate Judge on the ground that the defendant could not lead any evidence to prove her case that she got the money from her mother. Besides, according to the learned Subordinate Judge, it was highly improbable that such a big amount in cash would be kept with her for one year instead of depositing in the bank, because, Karirnunnessa died in 1950. It is not the case of that defendant that she received the entire amount of Rs. 28,830/- at a time.

21. According to the plaintiff he purchased the shares of 3 brothers Wazidur Rahman, Mazidur Rahman and Azizur Rahman in the aforesaid Dum Dum Road property in the name of defendant Nurjahan Begum. The share of Wazidur Rahman at 25, Dum Dum Road property was purchased by kabala Exhibit 1 (a) dated January 15, 1954 for Rs. 5,000/- and he purchased the share of Wazidur Rahman in the premises No. 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road by Kabala Exhibit 1(d) on the same date at R s. 3,000/- . He purchased the share of Mazidur Rahman in 25, Dum Dum Road property in the name of defendant for Rs. 5.000/- on February 26, 1954 and he purchased the share os Mazidur Rahman in 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road property in the name of the defendant. The share of Azizur Rahman in 25, Dum Dum Road property was purchased by him in the name of the defendant by kabala Exhibit 1(g) for Rs. 5,000/- and on the same date he purchased the share of Azizur Rahman in 23A and 23B, Dum Dum Road property for Rs. 3,000/- by kabala Exhibit 1(f). According to the defendant all the shares of her brothers were purchased by her with her own money. With regard to the shares of Azizur Rahman her case is that the shares of Azizur Rahman was not purchased by a regular sale but it was acquired by exchange with her Khulna property. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge disbelieved the case of the defendant regarding her purchase of all the shares of her three brothers Wazidur Rahman, Mazidur Rahman and Azizur Rahman in the Dum Dum Road property on the ground that she could not prove the source of money for the consideration of Rs. 16,000/- for acquiring the shares of Wazidur Rahman and Mazidur Rahman. He did not accept the defendant's case that to make up the deficiency in her fund she sold some of her ornaments for Rs. 8,000/- and that she could not produce any evidence to prove that she bad balance of the consideration money. The learned Subordinate Judge did not accept the defendant's case regarding her acquisition of the shares of Azizur Raman in the said properties by exchange of her Khulna property, on the ground that the relevant kabalas belied that it was not a case of sale.

According to the learned Subordinate Judge since she did not make out any case of purchase of the shares of Azizur Rahman as indicated by relevant kabalas, she was not entitled to lay any claim over that property. On perusal of the judgment it appears that the entire consideration was influenced by the finding that the defendant's father Kanchan Munshi had not the means to pay Rs. 50,000/- to the defendant for purchasing Park Street property in 1945, because at that time he was financially an exhausted man; and that defendant's mother Karimunessa Bibi, as the decree made against her for money in Suit No. 816 of 1943 shows that she had not the capacity to pay her creditors. It has already been discussed above that recovery of money was relating to labour charge for the work done in 1939 when a small sum of few hundreds remained due to the Contractor and he had to institute suit for recovery of the amount along with compensation. The decree Exhibit 20 shows that the entire claim in the suit was satisfied out of Court, and the suit was disposed of accordingly. Inability to pay the creditor on a particular day in 1939 for whatever reasons, cannot lead one to the conclusion that in 1945 both Karimunnessa Bibi and her husband Kanchan Munshi were in financially strained condition having not the capacity to make any gift, of money to their daughter in 1945. So far as the defendant's case of her acquiring shares of her full brother Azizur Rahman by exchange of her Khulna property is concerned, the learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the defendant s case only with reference to recitals in the kabalas Exhibit 1 (f) and 1(g) but without taking into consideration the relevant statement of Azizur Rahman himself on this point. On oath he stated that consideration of the kabala was the Khulna property of Nurjahan Begum given in exchange. Even the plaintiff admitted in cross examination that Aziz lives in Khuloa having exchanged a house there". True nature of the transaction may not be ascertained from the recitals in the kabalas Exhibit 1 (f) and 1 (g) but the evidence and the circumstances sufficiently indicate that the property in the shares of Azizur Rahman were exchanged with defendant's Khulna property, ownership of which is not disputed by the plaintiff. The letters Exhibits N, N1, N2, N3 and N4 written by the plaintiff to Azizur Rahman regarding the exchange of Azizur Rahman's share with that of the defendant in the Khulna property fully support the case of exchange as put forward by the defendant. Neither the learned Subordinate Judge nor the learned Judges of the High Court Division considered all the relevant materials on the question of purchase of shares of three brothers and three sisters in the Dum Dum Road properties by the defendant. The plaintiff cannot succeed with reference to the recitals in the kabalas alone. It is in the evidence that D.W. 2 Abu Md. Shikdar deposed that he negotiated the sales of the properties owned by three sisters. He stated that the vendors were paid Rs. 28, 800/- in his presence and it was agreed at the instance of Mr. Rafinddin Ahmed, pleader that they would pay the money to the plaintiff who in his turn would pay them in Pakistan by drafts. He further •stated. that after the consideration money of Rs. 28,800/- was paid by Nurjahan to her three sisters in Calcutta, they gave the money to the plaintiff on three receipts on the condition that he would pay them the same in Pakistan currency," and they, received three ban k drafts of Rs. 6,666/- each from the 'National Bank, Sadarghat. It is not disputed that the plaintiff was practically representing his wife for the purpose of completing the transactions.

22. With regard to the possession of the title Documents it is the case of plaintiff that the documents were stolen by the defendant taking advantages of his short absence from Ruplal House. According to him the documents were kept in an almirah at 12. Farashganj, Road, Dhaka where they were living together. The learned Subordinate Judge has not given any importance to the fact that all the relevant documents relating to, properties in suit were produced by the defendant and the plaintiff produced only some certified copies of the relevant title deeds. In support of the case, of the plaintiff that the documents were removed by the defendant during his absence, he produced a copy of the information lodged with the Sutrapur Police Station dated September 27, 1962 (Exhibit 7). In Exhibit 7 there is no particular reference to any removal of his title deeds as alleged by him in the plaint although he stated that he was compelled to leave his residence leaving behind all his valuable articles and belongings for safety of his life. On account of' this marriage his relationship with the defendant became strained and he started living in a separate house at Mitford Road.

In his deposition, however, he stated that price of schedule 'A' property 	was assessed at Rs. 1,00,000/- and price of the Park Street property was assessed at Rs. 55,000/- which was set off against the price of the schedule 'A' property and the balance Rs 40,000/- was paid in cash and Rs. 5000/- was adjusted against the earnest money paid in respect of this property. As per terms of the agreement transfer of RupIal House was completed by the registered kabala Exhibit A(3) eight annas share in favour of the defendant and eight annas share in favour of the plaintiff, and two others-Golam Rahman' Mullick and Azizur Rahman Mullick. Recitals in the kabala clearly show that the defendant acquired eight annas interest in 'A' schedule property for herself irf exchange of her Park Street property and partly in cash. Exhibits (1) Act) and A(2), the three sale deeds executed by Maran Chand in favour of the defendant transferring the entire property describe in schedule 'B', clearly show that the defendant was the purchaser. All the three sale deeds show that the amounts mentioned in the documents were retained and set off by the purchaser being due to her on account of the price of part of premises No. 23A, 23B and 25 Dum Dum Road;

<u>24. With regard to motive for purchasing the Park Street property and the Dum Dum Road\properties in the name of the defendant and subsequently acquiring 'A' schedule and  'B' schedule properties in exchange of Calcutta properties, the plaintiff did not give any explanation. Of course, motive in a case of banami is not always material but in some cases motive becomes an important factor in the determination of dispute relating to property acquired in banami. The learned Subordinate Judge while discussing the question of motive took resourse to speculation as to what might be the motive for acquiring the property by the plaintiff in the benami of his wife. He observed as follows:</u>

<u>"As I was telling that the plaintiff had vast business and other landed properties be took it into his head to take the documents in the name of his wife might be to defraud Income-Tax Authorities, because, if the properties were taken in his name that would add to his asset and income he already had and that would entail a huge Income Tax. Even if he had no such motive, he was free to take the documents in the name of his wife……………………….".</u>

<u>He, however, concluded with the following findings:</u>

<u>"Therefore, I have no hesitation to find that the parties being husband and wife in best of the terms and the husband being a business man having other properties thought it fit to take the documents in the name of his dear wife and on that account it cannot be said that the properties belong to the wife":</u>

<u>It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge made the above observation little thinking that a transaction in aid of an illegal device to defraud the Government cannot be taken as a valid ground in a proceeding before a Court of law.</u>

25. Now let me examine the question of possession of the properties acquired by the defendant, that is the Park Street property and the Dum Dum Road properties in 1945 and 1954 respectively; and the 'A' schedule and 'B' schedule properties in Dacca acquired in exchange of the Calcutta properties. This discussion will also cover the subsequent conduct of the, parties. According, to the plaintiff he was possessing the suit properties described in schedules 'A' and 'R' to plaint by collecting rent and paying government revenues, repairing the houses at his own expenses According to him he paid taxes and electricity hills. He asserted that he did everything in the name of the defendant in whose name the property stands. The defendant claimed that as the properties were acquired by her, name was mutated in the rent-roll of the Government Sherista; and she collected rent from the tenants; and she paid taxes and electricity bills and did all acts of possession independent of the plaintiff. She stated that as she pays income tax, she submits Income Tax Returns in her own name showing the income and expenditure. The defendant in support of her claim produced a number of documents. In the mutation case prayer of the defendant for correcting the records relating to Ruplal House wherein name of the previous owner that is Ramanath Das appeared, the plaintiff Mahmudur Rahman Mullick did not file any objection. He however, seriously opposed the defendant's application for separation of Rent Account. The order-sheet Exhibit I shows that the Revenue Authority overruled the objection by a long judgment. Portions of it are quoted below:

(b) "Khatian has been opened and finally published as per deed as such if there is any objection against the recording the defendants ought to have filed an objection in the Settlement Department but they did not do that. Over and above it appears from the Income Tax Assessment Roll that the plaintiff and the defendants paid the income tax according to their share and cleared up Municipal dues accordingly".

(c) "The properties were purchased jointly in the year 1954 and I cannot understand as to why the defendants (that is plaintiff in the suit) raised objection after long 9 years. I cannot go against this finally published records unless it will be declared by the Court of judicature at 'Benamdar".

The Revenue officer by his order dated 30.10.63 accorded sanction to the sub-division of the holding. It does not appear that the plaintiff took the matter by way of an appeal to the superior Revenue Authority. In support of the defendant's case that she collected rents from the tenants in the premises, she produced the relevant papers to show that rents were realised in the name of the defendant and separate account was maintained therefor. Regarding the incomes from the suit property and other properties owned by the defendant, separate Income Tax Returns were filed and she used to appear before the Income Tax Officer in support of her case.

Exhibits K series show that for the assessment years 1955-56 to 1963-64 incomes were separately, assessed and the assesse. Nurjahan Begum appeared herself before the Income Tax Officer. The Income Tax Officer in the assessment order for the assessment year 1955-56 treated the defendant as the owner of the half share of the Ruplal House and made the assessment order accordingly. Exhibit K(2) assessment order dated April 14. 1959 for the assessment year 1958-59 shows that the Income Tax Authority accepted the defendant as the assesse having income from house property, that is, 8 annas share in Rupial House. It also shows that collection charge was allowed which was paid to defendant's agents for collecting rent. From the assessment orders it appears that the defendant Nurjahan Begum appeared personally with her books of accounts, sometimes along with her husband, but as a separate assesse. The assessment orders support her case that the properties described in schedules 'A' and  'B' were acquired by her in exchange of her property in Calcutta and she treated the properties as her own. She produced a copy of the income tax assessment order made against her in Calcutta before the Income Tax Officer. The assessment orders show that the books of accounts and counterfoils of rent receipts fully satisfied the Income-Tax Officer for accepting the defendant's case that she was the actual owner in possession of the properties acquired by her in exchange of her Calcutta properties.

26. In this context some correspondence between the defendant and her lawyer Indra Chandra Ghosh, Solicitor, Calcutta and plaintiff Mahmudur Rahman Mullick lend sufficient support to the defendant's case that the properties in suit were acquired by the defendant in exchange of her property in India. Letters from the Solicitor Exhibits N(9), N(10), N(11), N(12), N(13), N(14), N(15), N(16), N(17), N(18) and N(19) clearly show that the Solicitor was sending reminders after reminders to the defendant for payment of his outstanding dues. The letters show that the Solicitor acted in the matters of exchange of properties. Language in the letters is very clear to show that the Solicitor was asking for payment of his dues from the defendant and the demand was not made through the plaintiff. These letters fully support the case of the defendant that the property in suit were acquired for her own benefit.

27. The defendant examined some of her tenants at the trial D.W. 3 Chand Mea, an `Aratdar' at 12 Shyam Bazar stated that he was a tenant since the time of the predecessor of the defendant namely, Ramanath Das, and on the basis of a letter requesting him to pay rent to the defendant and three Mallik Brothers, he was paying them rent accordingly. He stated that he pays 8 annas rent to Nurjanaa and remaining 8 annas to Mallik Brothers, He produced two rent receipts mc of which was granted by Nujahan under her signature anti the other was\granted by Azizur Rahman Mullick. The rent receipts were marked Exhibits G(12) and G(13). He also proved his signatures on the counterfoils of corresponding rent receipts and the signature was marked as Exhibit V. D.W. 5 Nani Gopal Basak proved that he is a tenant under Nurjahan Begum in respect of his shop at 51, English Road. He used to pay her rent. He proved his signatures in the counterfoils Exhibits V(1), V(2) and V(3). He also stated that on the basis of a notice given by Maran Chand Sen, the previous owner of the property, he has been paying rent to Nurjahan Begum. He proved the notice Exhibit W.

28. On consideration of the evidence both oral and documentary I have no doubt that the suit property as described is schedules 'A' and 'B' are being managed by the defendant herself. She maintains accounts separately, pays income tax and government revenues. She also pays Municipal taxes, etc.

29. In consideration of the evidence sup-porting the defendant's case I am constrained to hold that the learned Judges of the High Court Division affirmed the judgments of the trial Court without proper and independent assessment of the evidence. I find that the plaintiff failed to rebutt the presumption that the vendee as shown in the registered documents of transfer is the person who acquired the property and is the beneficiary of the same. The learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division without taking into consideration the relevant materials on record which amply show that the property in suit were being managed by the owner, that is, the defendant herself and that the plaintiff failed to discharge the onus that heavily lay upon him. On this question the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the Learned Judges of the High Court Division committed serious error in procedure sufficient to vitiate their decision, in as much as, the defendant was saddled with the burden to prove that she is not the benamdar of the plaintiff in respect of the properties in suit.

30. Mr. M. H. Khondkar strenuously argued that in view of clear admission of the plaintiff in Title Suit No.163 and 183 of, 1949 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge; Alipore, West Bengal (India) in his written statement filed in Title Suit No. 183 of 1949 (Exhibit Z3 (1); in the petition of objection affirmed by his affidavit Exhibit Z2 (I) filed in Title Suit No. 163 of 1949 resisting the application for appointment of receiver (Exhibit) ZI(1); in the Solenama Exhibit P filed in Title Suit No. 163 of 1949. which formed part of the preliminary decree Exhibit O(1). and Final Decree Exhibit 0 made in Title Suit No. 163 of 1949; and in the written statement, filed in Title Suit No. 183 of 1949 wherein No. 207A, Park Street property was also included, 'the plaintiff is estopped from making any claim over the self-same property to have been acquired by him with his own fund and for his own benefit. To lend support to his argument the learned Advocate with reference to some of the evidence led by the defendant supporting her possession in the suit property submitted that in the absence of any evidence that the properties acquired by exchange were ever treated by the plaintiff as his own and 'he possessed' the same, the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division Clearly misdirected themselves in declaring the defendant as the benamdar of the plaintiff in respect of 8 annas share of the properties described in schedule 'A' to the plaint and 14 83/104 annas share of the properties described in schedule 'B' to the plaint; and confirming plaintiff's possession in' those properties other than the residence portion of 12, Farashganj Road, Dacca; and allowing joint possession in the said residence portion with the defendant. In this context the learned Advocate further submitted with reference to the application filed by the plaintiff in the First Appeal No. 140 of 1965 preferred by the defendant against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court that the plaintiff's statement made therein clearly shows that the defendant has been in possession of the suit properties. The learned Advocate in elucidating this point argued that the plaintiff prayed for declaration of his ownership in the suit properties" and a negative declaration that the defendant has no possession therein; and in the alternative prayed for khas possession if he be found out of possession. In his evidence the plaintiff stated that the property (schedule 'B') "is still in my possession and on realisation of rents". By the decree plaintiff's possession in the 'A' and 'B' schedule properties other than" the residence portion of 12, "Farashganj Road ('A' schedule) was con- firmed, but about two years after filing of the First Appeal by the defendant against the said judgment and decree the plaintiff filed an application on February 14, 1967 before the High Court for appointment of a Receiver of the suit properties. The said application was rejected by the High Court by the order dated April 12, 1967 with the following observation:

"It is rather curious that the petitioner who claims to be in possession of the said properties and who has obtained a decree for confirmation of possession should have come and asked for appointment of a Receiver unless the position is something other than what was alleged in the suit".

31. The learned Advocate in criticising the judgment of the High Court Division submitted that while affirming unsustainable findings of the trial Court the learned Judges of the High Court Division even did not take notice of the Court's own order dated April 12, 1967. According to the learned Advocate if the learned Judges took pains to look into the application filed by the plaintiff (or appointment of a Receiver for the suit properties after obtaining decree of confirmation of his possession from the trial Court, and the order of the Court rejecting the prayer, the decision in the appeal might have been different.

32. Title Suit No. 163 of 1949 was fired by the three sisters of the defendant, namely, Amina Begum, Megar Bibi and Sakhina Khatun and brother Bazlur Rahman. Defendant's brother's Mazidur Rahman, Wazidur Rahman, Azizur Rahman and the defendant herself and one sister Jahanara Begum were impleaded as parties in that suit for partition. The suit was instituted on September 21, 1949. Subsequently Ayatunnessa Bibi, wife of late Kanchan Munshi and Mahmudur Rahman Mullick (the present plaintiff)' were added as parties to the suit. The suit properties amongst others included the Dum Dum Road properties and the Park Street properties. While deposing at the trial the plaintiff in cross-examination stated that the above mentioned two title suits were tried analogously and were disposed of by the same solenama. He admitted that the statements embodied in paragraphs 3 and 9 of the solenama were made by him; and the suit was dismissed against him in terms of the solenama. He also admitted that Park Street property was added the schedule to the plaint before he filed written statement and affidavit-in-opposition to the application for appointment of Receiver in respect of the suit properties. He also admitted that be made the statement in the petition of compromise that holding No. 207A Park Street was the exclusive and self acquired property of Nurjahan Begum and that excepting herself none of the parties to that suit had any share in the same. In the written statement Exhibit Z3(1) filed on December 23, 1950 in Title Suit No. 183 of 1949 the present plaintiff stated as under-

"Premises No. 207 now 207A, Park Street, Calcutta comprising 8 cottas of Nisbkar land rent free. were purchased by the defendant No. 4 Nurjahan Begum from Shaikh Nasiruddin with money paid and advanced by her husband this defendant and she has been in possession thereof since the date of purchase adversely and to the exclusion of Kanchan Munshi (father of Nurjahan Begum) and his heirs".

I find there is sufficient force in the submissions of the learned Advocate.

33. Title Suit No. 183 of 1949 was filed by Bazlur Rahman and others impleading Mazidur Rahman and others for partition of the properties purchased by Kanchan Munshi. In this Suit also premises 207A, Park Street, Calcutta was included, In Title Suit No 163 of 1949 a petition under Order X, rule 1 Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of receiver was filed by defendant No. 7 of that suit. The present plaintiff Mahmudur Rahman Mullick Died a petition of objection opposing the prayer (or appointment of Receive in respect of Premises No. 207A, Park Street. "In those I stated that though the Park Street properties were acquired by me with my money those properties belonged exclusively to her. My case was the same from filing of the suits till compromise".

34. In paragraph 3 of the compromise petition it was stated that the parties to the solenama admitted that the property included at item 9 in the list of immovable properties of the amended plaint means the land at 207, at present 207A, Park Street containing an area of 8 cottas, 5 chhataks and 15 square feet has been the exclusive self- acquired property of defendant No.4 Nurjahan Begum. In this property excepting defendant No. 4 Nurjahan Begum none of the other parties have any kind of share nor had any claims nor have or shall have any. In the compromise petition in paragraph 16 it was stated that Title Suit No. 183 of 1949 filed by Bazlur Rahman was also compromised in terms of this solenama, etc. Both the suits were disposed of as per terms of the solenama which formed part of the preliminary decree Exhibit-O(1) and final decree-Exhibit-O. Plaintiff's attention was drawn to his statement made in his written statement filed in Title Suit No. 163 or 1949 and paragraph 3 of the compromise petition filed by the parties therein. The plaintiff stated as follows:-

"These properties of Park Street were added before I filed W.S. In the W.S. and in the affidavit in opposition to the application for appointment of Receiver in those I stated that though the Park Street properties were acquired by me with my' money those properties belonged exclusively to her. My case was the same from filing of the suits till compromise.

''In paragraph 3 of the petition of compromise filed in Title Suit Nos. 163 and 18 of 1949 whatever is written there is true. I made statement therein that holding No. 207A, Park Street was the exclusive and self-acquired property of Nurjahan Begum and excepting herself none of the parties to that suit had any share in the same".

35. With regard to his statement made in the written statement the plaintiff admitted that he filed a written statement but when a certified copy of it was shown to him he could not say if it was this, he, however, stated that in that suit a solenama was filed and without reading the solenama he signed the statements made by the plaintiff in the above mentioned title suits.

36.The statements made in the said suits are relevant for adjudication of the issue- "Is the suit barred by principle of estoppel, waiver, acquiescence and conduct ?" Certified copies of the preliminary decree and final decree made in the said suits are admissible in evidence for determining the ownership of the suit properties. From the judgments of the trial Court and that of the High Court Division it does not appear that any serious consideration was given to this aspect of the case. The suits being partition suits wherein the present plaintiff and defendant were impleaded as parties, the decrees having been passed therein in their presence, they are bound by the same. The statements made in the solenama, upon which the suits were disposed of carry a legal presumption that the statements were consciously made. However, the presumption is rebuttable but the plaintiff did not offer any explanation by way of rebuttal. The learned Counsel has correctly submitted that in absence of any evidence rebutting the presumption, the admissions are binding upon the plaintiff. With regard to subsequent conduct of the parties it has been found that it was the defendant who was although exercising her right as the owner in possession and the plaintiff could not produce any evidence to support his case of exercising his right to possession in the suit properties. In my opinion the plaintiff is estopped from challenging the title of the defendant in the suit properties calling her as his benamdar,

<u>37. Before concluding I like to observe that in the case of benami transactions, although the source of purchase money is an important criteria but it is not conclusive where there are other circumstances showing that the purchaser intended the property to belong to the person in whose favour the sale deed is executed. So it is the intention of the parties which practically determines the question as to who is the owner of the property. It has been already noticed that the defendant succeeded in showing that she had the capacity to pay the consideration for the properties acquired by her and the sale deeds were executed in her favour. In this context reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Kanakarathanammal v V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 S.C. 271, In this case the question for consideration was whether in transaction where purchase was made by the wife and consideration money was paid by the husband, wife shall be treated as the benamdar of her husband in respect of the property purchased by her. In determining this question subsequent conduct of the parties was taken into consideration; and mainly on consideration of the conduct of the parties regarding possession of the property, the statements made by the husband on different occasions in respect of the properties in suit it has been held that the property had been purchased by the wife in her own name though the consideration which was paid by her had been received by her from her husband. From the reported case it appears that the learned Judges while examining the question of benami remarked that the High Court did not correctly appreciate the effect of the admissions made by the husband. The finding of the trial Court, approved by the High Court was reversed. In the instant case position is more or less the same. What is the effect of the admission made by the plaintiff in Title Suit Nos. 163 and 183 of 1949 has not been properly appreciated. Admissibility of the written statement filed by the plaintiff in. the above mentioned title suits and his statement in the petition of objection filed by him to oppose the petition for appointment of Receiver and the statement made in the solenama to which he was a party, has not been disputed. In the absence of rebuttal of the presumption that the admissions were consciously made by the plaintiff, in law his admission operates against him in his claim against his wife over the suit property which were acquired by exchange of the Park Street and Dum Dum Road properties. In short, the plaintiff is estopped from putting up the claim that the properties were acquired by hem for himself and that the defendant was his benamdar.</u>

38. The law of benami has not been properly applied to the facts of this case by either the learned Subordinate Judge or the learned Judges of the High Court Division. In the absence of proper application of the law of benami the course of justice has been misdirected, and because of this, notwithstanding the concurrent finding of facts it called for examination of the evidence. It has been already mentioned above that the trial Court accepting the plaintiff's case that the suit properties were acquired in the benami of the defendant and the judgment of the High Court Division affirming the same are mainly based on the conclusion deduced from the source of the consideration money but the materials on record do not warrant the findings. The question of benami, in the facts and circumstances of this case, has not been correctly decided on proper application of the law of benami. So, the judgments in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained. In the result the appeal is allowed Judgment and decree of the trial Court and those of the High Court Division are set aside and the suit is dismissed with costs.

End.
